prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff passenger.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that the Montreal Convention's two-year limitations period is a condition precedent to suit that may nonetheless be affected by equitable considerations, or alternatively the airline's bankruptcy stay tolls it.

Cite at least six decisions of the Eleventh Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

**I. Article 35 Is a Condition Precedent to Suit, but Its Operation Is Governed by Forum Law, Including Equitable Principles.**

Article 35(1) of the Montreal Convention provides that the "right to damages shall be extinguished if an action is not brought within a period of two years." Convention for the Unification of Certain Rules for International Carriage by Air art. 35(1), May 28, 1999, S. Treaty Doc. No. 106-45. Plaintiff does not dispute that this language makes timely suit a condition of the right to recover. But Article 35(2) adds that "[t]he method of calculating that period shall be determined by the law of the court seized of the case." *Id.* art. 35(2). That clause incorporates the forum's own rules on when the period runs, pauses, or is excused. The label "condition precedent" therefore does not end the inquiry.

Some courts have treated Article 35 as immune from tolling. *See, e.g.*, *Narayanan v. British Airways*, 747 F.3d 1125 (9th Cir. 2014). Those decisions are not binding here, and they give Article 35(2) too little weight. The Supreme Court's refusal to apply equitable tolling to the Hague Convention's one-year period in *Lozano v. Montoya Alvarez*, 572 U.S. 1, 10–15 (2014), rested on that treaty's text, structure, and purpose. Article 35(2) expressly delegates the calculation method to forum law, which distinguishes it from the provision in *Lozano*.

Forum law in this Circuit recognizes equitable tolling as a general doctrine. The Eleventh Circuit applies it where "extraordinary circumstances that are both beyond [the litigant's] control and unavoidable even with diligence" cause an untimely filing. *Sandvik v. United States*, 177 F.3d 1269, 1271 (11th Cir. 1999); *see also Justice v. United States*, 6 F.3d 1474, 1479 (11th Cir. 1993) (recognizing tolling where a plaintiff was prevented from timely filing by circumstances outside his control). The court has applied the doctrine in federal civil litigation, *Bost v. Fed. Express Corp.*, 372 F.3d 1233, 1242 (11th Cir. 2004), and in claims with an international dimension, *Arce v. Garcia*, 434 F.3d 1254, 1261–62 (11th Cir. 2006). It has also stressed that the inquiry is fact-specific and turns on diligence and the extraordinary character of the obstacle. *Steed v. Head*, 219 F.3d 1298, 1300 (11th Cir. 2000). The Supreme Court likewise treats the doctrine as a background rule of general application. *Holland v. Florida*, 560 U.S. 631, 645–49 (2010).

Plaintiff acted diligently. The carrier's insolvency proceedings, which Plaintiff did not cause and could not control, made it impossible to proceed against the carrier in the ordinary course. Applying Article 35(2), this Court should hold that the two-year period is subject to equitable tolling under Eleventh Circuit law. At a minimum, it should reverse the dismissal and remand for findings on diligence and extraordinary circumstances.

**II. Alternatively, the Airline's Bankruptcy Stay Tolled the Period.**

Even if equitable tolling were unavailable, the automatic stay independently suspended the limitations period. Filing a bankruptcy petition operates as a stay of "the commencement or continuation" of any judicial action against the debtor that was or could have been commenced before the petition. 11 U.S.C. § 362(a)(1). The Eleventh Circuit reads the stay broadly, as a fundamental protection that gives the debtor a breathing spell, and treats actions taken in violation of it as without effect. *Jove Eng'g, Inc. v. IRS*, 92 F.3d 1539, 1546, 1553–55 (11th Cir. 1996); *see also Eskanos & Adler, P.C. v. Leetien*, 309 F.3d 1210, 1213–14 (11th Cir. 2002). Plaintiff could not have filed suit against the debtor carrier without violating that stay.

Congress has also addressed the timing consequences. If a nonbankruptcy law fixes a period for commencing a suit against a debtor and that period has not expired before the petition is filed, the period does not expire until the later of the original date or 30 days after notice of termination of the stay. 11 U.S.C. § 108(c). Because Article 35(2) directs the court to apply forum law in calculating the period, § 108(c) and the stay are part of that calculation. They do not alter the treaty's substance. They are the "method of calculating" the two years, applied by the "court seized of the case." A plaintiff who was legally barred from suing during the stay should not lose the right to damages because of the stay.

Under either route, the two-year period had not expired when Plaintiff sued, and the district court's contrary ruling should be reversed.

*[Cite-check note: Confirm all pin cites and subsequent history before filing. I have not located an Eleventh Circuit F.3d decision squarely deciding whether Article 35 is subject to tolling, so Part I relies on general Eleventh Circuit tolling authority and Article 35(2).]*
